title: Christmas Day (John 1:1–18)
hookLine: the day Mass reads the Word made flesh

cards: Come back to church on Christmas morning, and something odd happens. The gospel has no manger. No shepherds, no angels, no star, no donkey, no inn.

Mary isn't named, and Bethlehem isn't mentioned. The reader starts before the world existed, with three words that echo the first line of Genesis: in the beginning. The night Mass told what happened in a stable.
The day Mass tells who was born there.

teach.b: Nativity comes from the Latin nativitas, a birth, and the Church's formal name for December 25 is the Nativity of the Lord. Its daytime gospel is the prologue of John, eighteen verses that read like a poem.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Word, in Greek, is logos: speech, reason, the meaning behind things.
John says this Word made everything, and the life in him was the light of people.
"And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Comprehend can mean understand, or grasp, even overpower; the Greek allows both, and translators still differ.
Then the line the whole day turns on: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh, not spirit dressed up as a man: skin, hunger, a body that could get cold.

teach.h: HE PITCHED HIS TENT AMONG US.
teach.b: Dwelt literally means pitched a tent, the way God's presence lived in a tent among the Israelites in the desert. Catholics mark this line with their bodies.

At the Creed each Sunday, people bow at the words about the incarnation; on Christmas and on the Annunciation, they kneel. Luke and John tell the same Christmas from two ends. Luke says: here is a baby, laid in a trough.
John says: that baby is the Word that was there in the beginning. Put them together and you have the whole surprise of the day.

how: At the Mass during the Day on Christmas, Catholics hear the prologue of John's Gospel, and at the Creed the congregation kneels at the words about the incarnation.

s: the Christmas day gospel has the shepherds
it's John's prologue: no manger, no shepherds, just in the beginning.
Catholics kneel at the Creed on Christmas
at the words about the incarnation, on Christmas and the Annunciation.
dwelt among us, in the Greek, pictures a tent
the Word pitched his tent among us.

games.q: you're writing a gospel. you could start Jesus's story at his birth, or his baptism. where does John start?
games.why: in the beginning was the Word. John goes back before the world, then says that Word was made flesh.

practice: Visit a nativity scene, in a church, a store window, a neighbor's yard or on a shelf at home, or picture one you remember; Saint Francis of Assisi is said to have set up a living one at Greccio, with a real ox and donkey, so people could see how poor the birth was.
Look at the smallest figure. If you pray, say John's line, the Word was made flesh; if not, just look.

wordCard.voice: Nativity. From the Latin for birth; the Church's name for Christmas, the Nativity of the Lord, when the Word was made flesh. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the Word became flesh, John 1:14.

carryVoice: Your line: the word made flesh. Merry Christmas, wherever you're spending it. See you tomorrow.
